title: TPG and Corpay to take fintech BILL private in $6 billion deal
summary: BILL Holdings has agreed to be acquired by private equity firm TPG in partnership with Corpay for $63.25 a share in cash, a deal worth about $6 billion that ends months of activist pressure on the San Jose fintech.
content:
Fintech company BILL Holdings has agreed to be taken private in a deal worth about $6 billion, ending months of pressure from activist investors and marking one of the largest software buyouts of the year.

BILL, the San Jose-based financial operations platform used by nearly 500,000 businesses, said on Thursday it had entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by private equity firm TPG in partnership with Corpay, the global spend management company. Shareholders will receive $63.25 per share in cash, a price that values the company at approximately $6.0 billion on a fully diluted basis, according to [the companies' announcement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261119835477/en/BILL-Agrees-to-be-Acquired-by-TPG-in-Partnership-with-Corpay).

The offer represents a premium of about 31 percent to BILL's 60-day volume-weighted average share price through November 16, the last full trading session before reports of the talks surfaced. The transaction was approved unanimously by BILL's board and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to approval by shareholders and regulators.

TPG will acquire a majority interest in BILL through TPG Capital, its U.S. and European private equity platform, while Corpay will take a minority stake. Corpay said it would invest $1.1 billion for roughly a one-third equity interest, with an option to acquire the rest of the company in 2030. Corpay expects the deal to add to its cash earnings per share in 2027.

The agreement caps a difficult stretch for BILL, whose shares have fallen far from the highs of the pandemic-era software boom as growth slowed and investors soured on loss-making fintech. Earlier this year the company announced plans to cut about 30 percent of its workforce as part of a restructuring aimed at restoring profitability.

Activist pressure helped force the outcome. Starboard Value, BILL's largest shareholder with an 8.5 percent stake, disclosed its position earlier this year and nominated directors to the board; Reuters has also reported interest from Elliott Investment Management. Starboard has agreed to vote its shares in favour of the $63.25-a-share deal, removing one of the main obstacles to a sale.

For Corpay, the deal is a calculated step into the market for small and mid-sized business payments. The Atlanta-based company, best known for corporate payment and fleet cards, gains access to BILL's large base of business customers and its accounts-payable and receivable software, which it can cross-sell alongside its own products. The structure, with a staged path to full ownership in 2030, lets Corpay test that fit before committing to the whole business.

Investors gave the announcement a cautious reception. BILL's shares fell about 3.7 percent in after-hours trading, a sign that some shareholders had hoped for a higher price or worry about the long road to closing, which stretches into the first half of next year and requires both shareholder and regulatory approval.

BILL, founded in 2006 as Bill.com, built its business automating invoicing, bill payment and expense management for small and medium-sized companies, a market long underserved by traditional banks. The company says its platform moves billions of dollars a year on behalf of its customers, and it has expanded through acquisitions, including the purchase of expense-management firm Divvy in 2021.

Under private ownership, BILL will be delisted from the New York Stock Exchange. TPG has not said whether it plans further restructuring, but buyout firms typically use the privacy of private ownership to cut costs and reposition a company away from the quarterly scrutiny of public markets. For BILL's customers, the companies said it would be business as usual, with the platform continuing to operate and Corpay's investment funding product development.

The deal is the latest in a wave of take-private transactions in software, as private equity firms move in on listed companies whose valuations have fallen sharply since 2021. With interest rates still elevated and public-market investors demanding profits rather than growth, many mid-sized software firms have found themselves valued below what buyers are willing to pay. The [global market sell-off](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026) that has hit technology shares this week underlines how fragile that confidence remains.

What happens next will be watched closely. Shareholders must vote on the deal, and regulators will review it, but the unanimous board backing and Starboard's support make approval likely. The bigger question is whether the combination delivers: Corpay must show that its minority investment can be turned into a full acquisition in 2030 at a price that rewards both sides, while TPG must prove that a business built on steady, unglamorous back-office software can grow fast enough to justify a $6 billion price tag. The [wave of corporate upheaval](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/japan-tobacco-8-9-billion-charge-russia-seizure-november-2026) hitting big companies this year suggests buyers believe it can, as [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/bill-holdings-be-taken-private-by-tpg-6-billion-equity-value-2026-11-19/).
